summary:
Voronezh Oblast stands under the Russian national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. The source inventory identifies no Voronezh-specific deviation material enough to score separately, so the oblast is assessed at the Russian national score.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year and gender-marker changes on official documents are now prohibited. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute criminalises any public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the Russian national government has explicitly warned LGBT travellers of this; the US State Department carries a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Russia that contains warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court "extremist" designation of the international LGBT movement, participation in the designated movement carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Document markers cannot be corrected, so any police, hotel or transport identity check in the oblast reads a mismatch between a visitor's papers and their presentation.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Human Rights Watch counted about 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions among the 101 extremism-related cases as of 30 June 2025; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Physical coercion is documented alongside state action. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition, gender-marker changes and trans-specific healthcare that applies to visitors, with no lawful route to correct documents after transition. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but relationship recognition and gender transition are unavailable.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia for sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that the Russian state is able but not willing to protect openly LGBT+ people from discriminatory treatment.

The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Displaying symbols of the designated movement is prosecuted under Article 20.3 as an administrative offence; 81 people were found guilty in 98 such cases, with fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals, while repeat offending under the propaganda statutes escalates to up to four years' imprisonment. Organising activity within the designated movement is charged under Article 282.2 and carries 6-10 years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Voronezh Oblast-specific enforcement record appears in the source inventory: whether courts in the oblast have issued convictions under Article 282.2 or Article 20.3, and in what numbers, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory identifies no oblast-level variation in policing practice, no local clinics, support organisations or venues in Voronezh, and no oblast-specific government statements on gender identity. Their existence or absence is not sourced.

The date of the most recent assessment covering Voronezh Oblast directly is not established; the national framework described rests on sources dated between June 2025 and August 2026, and no source tests whether enforcement in the oblast diverges from the national pattern in either direction.

The UK Home Office figures for people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws cover Russia as a whole and are not broken down by federal subject, so no oblast-level share can be derived from them.
